it: MERCY WITHOUT BLOOD IN THE BIBLE

JESUS WAY 065 · Why Christians HATE Jesus' Real Salvation Teachings

With Nathaniel Jordan (Minister of Wellness). From The Jesus Way, Aaron Abke and James Benefico's podcast. Posted 2026-08-20.

Aaron, James and returning guest Nathaniel Jordan argue that Jesus taught salvation by mercy, service and keeping the commandments, and that blood sacrifice (animal or atoning) misrepresents God. They read Old Testament violence (Amalek, Jephthah) and Pauline passages (Romans 9, 2 Corinthians 12) as evidence of corruption in scripture, drawing on the Clementine Homilies' doctrine of 'false pericopes' and on the Gospel of the Holy Twelve and Essene Gospel of Peace. Much of the episode is also a fundraising appeal for Nathaniel's feeding and orphan ministry in Kenya.

HOW TO READ THIS BOARD: each grey card is a moment from the episode, with its time; ▶ opens the video there. Beside it is the check, and beside that the evidence, tied by string. Click any card to read it.

no blood offering of beast or bird or man can take away sin

~ NARROWER

Jesus taught that no blood offering of beast, bird or man can take away sin, as recorded in the Gospel of the Holy Twelve.

The words are in the Gospel of the Holy Twelve, which G. J. R. Ouseley serialised in a Lincolnshire newspaper from 1898 to 1901. Its claimed ancient Tibetan manuscript has never been produced, so the text tells us what Ouseley wrote, not what Jesus said. The canonical record has a narrower version of the theme: Jesus twice quotes Hosea 6:6, 'I will have mercy, and not sacrifice'.
The Gospel of the Holy Twelve (Wikipedia)
has never been produced or proven to exist
The Gospel of the Holy Twelve (Wikipedia), citing Richard Alan Young
It appears that Ouseley created The Gospel of the Holy Twelve in support of animal welfare and vegetarianism.
cease ye from the eating of flesh. Which is what that passage in Jeremiah originally stated

✗ DOESN'T HOLD

Jeremiah 7:21 originally said 'cease ye from the eating of flesh', and God says he never commanded sacrifices at the Exodus.

Jeremiah 7:22-23 does say God did not command burnt offerings or sacrifices when he brought Israel out of Egypt, only 'Obey my voice'. That part holds. But verse 21 reads 'Put your burnt offerings unto your sacrifices, and eat flesh' in the KJV, and the Jewish JPS translation has 'eat the meat!'. No known Hebrew or Greek manuscript reads 'cease from eating flesh'; that wording is the Gospel of the Holy Twelve's. Jeremiah 33:18 also promises Levites to offer burnt offerings, and most readers take 7:22 as ranking obedience above sacrifice rather than denying the sacrificial law outright.
Add your burnt offerings to your other sacrifices and eat the meat!
this pagan practice of animal sacrifice, which is not a Jewish practice.

✗ DOESN'T HOLD

Animal sacrifice was a pagan practice brought in around the Babylonian exile and was never a Jewish practice.

Sacrifice was widespread in the ancient Near East before Israel, so 'it predates Judaism' holds. 'Not a Jewish practice' does not: the Torah legislates sacrifice in detail, and the Bible describes it at the First Temple long before the exile (1 Kings 8:63). The prophets' critiques also come from before the exile (Amos 5:22, Isaiah 1:11), and they presuppose sacrifice was being practised. Temple sacrifice continued until 70 CE.
The Torah contains many laws about sacrifices.
until the Second Temple was also destroyed in 70 CE.
And it it really comes down to the Babylonian exile. every time.

✗ DOESN'T HOLD

The Essenes split off around the Babylonian exile because they rejected animal sacrifice, and later flourished in the Transjordan.

Mainstream history places Essene origins in the Maccabean or Hasmonean period (2nd century BCE), centuries after the exile. Pliny puts them by the Dead Sea and Philo in the villages of Judea; Epiphanius (4th century) does put related groups, the Ossaeans and Nasaraeans, east of the Jordan, so the Transjordan part has some ancient support. Philo says they did not sacrifice living animals, but Qumran texts such as 4QMMT and the Temple Scroll legislate sacrifice, which points to a break with the Temple establishment rather than a rejection of sacrifice in principle. Josephus (Antiquities 18.1.5) cannot settle it either way: the key sentence turns on a negative that the manuscripts disagree about.
a sect which had existed in the time of the Maccabees
in the Hebrew Bible, repent and God forgives you. He wipes your sins out.

✓ HOLDS

The Hebrew Bible repeatedly says God forgives those who repent, and Jesus forgave sins before the cross.

The images cited are real: sins removed 'as far as the east is from the west' (Psalm 103:12) and cast 'into the depths of the sea' (Micah 7:19). Ezekiel 18:21-22 says a wicked man who turns 'shall surely live'. Jesus preached 'Repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand' (Matthew 4:17) and forgave the paralytic directly (Mark 2:5).
There is no verse anywhere in the Bible that even implies that if you sin once

~ NARROWER

No verse in the Bible says you must keep the law perfectly or be condemned; not even Paul taught this.

No verse says one sin makes forgiveness impossible. But the 'perfect law-keeping' argument does have verses behind it. Paul's Galatians 3:10 quotes Deuteronomy 27:26: 'Cursed is every one that continueth not in all things... to do them'. James 2:10 says whoever offends in one point 'is guilty of all', and Romans 3:20 says no flesh is justified by the deeds of the law. The narrower true claim is that none of these comes from Jesus, and none says repentance cannot bring forgiveness.
Maybe Jesus was serious when he said, "I desire mercy, not sacrifice."

✓ HOLDS

Jesus said 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice', and reading 'not' as 'and' is special pleading.

Jesus quotes Hosea 6:6 twice, at Matthew 9:13 and 12:7, both times against critics. The 'not means and' reading usually rests on the verse's second line, 'the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings', which is comparative. The first line is a flat 'not', and many scholars read the pair as a Hebrew idiom of priority. Both readings are argued; the quotation itself is solid.
If you want to enter eternal life, keep the commandments, thou shalt not kill.

✓ HOLDS

Jesus told a questioner that to enter eternal life he should keep the commandments, naming 'thou shalt not kill'.

Matthew 19:17-18: 'if thou wilt enter into life, keep the commandments... Thou shalt do no murder'. It is also in Mark 10:19 and Luke 18:20. Mainstream evangelical readings note that the passage goes on to 'sell that thou hast' (19:21), and many read the scene as exposing that no one can keep the law. That is an interpretation added to the text.
for I never knew you. For when I was hungry, you didn't feed me.

~ NARROWER

Jesus will say 'depart from me, I never knew you' to those who did not feed the hungry, and 'the least of these' plausibly includes animals.

Two passages are merged here. 'I never knew you: depart from me' is Matthew 7:23, addressed to people who prophesied in his name. 'I was an hungred, and ye gave me no meat' is the judgment scene of Matthew 25:41-43. Both are judgments on conduct rather than belief, which is the hosts' point. Extending 'the least of these' to animals is their interpretation; the text says 'the least of these my brethren' (25:40).
It's easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for the law to pass away.

✓ HOLDS

Jesus said his words will never pass away and that it is easier for heaven and earth to pass than for the law to fail.

Luke 16:17: 'it is easier for heaven and earth to pass, than one tittle of the law to fail'. Matthew 5:18 has the jot-and-tittle form, and Matthew 24:35 has 'my words shall not pass away'. Christians who see the law as completed point to Matthew 5:18's own clause, 'till all be fulfilled', so the interpretive fight is over that phrase rather than over what Jesus said.
I take them right to 1st Samuel chapter 15 verse 1 through3

✓ HOLDS

1 Samuel 15:1-3 commands the killing of Amalekite infants and sucklings, about 400 years after Amalek attacked Israel leaving Egypt.

1 Samuel 15:3 reads 'slay both man and woman, infant and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and ass', citing what Amalek did 'when he came up from Egypt' (15:2; Exodus 17:8; Deuteronomy 25:17-18). The roughly 400-year gap (raised at 17:56) fits the Bible's own chronology, since 1 Kings 6:1 puts Solomon's temple 480 years after the Exodus.
in the book of Judges chap 11 and everybody can read this for themselves

~ NARROWER

In Judges 11, under the Spirit of the LORD, Jephthah vowed a burnt offering and then burned his daughter, and the text clearly says so.

The judge is Jephthah, not Jethro, though the auto-captions may be at fault. The Spirit comes on him (11:29), he vows a burnt offering (11:31), and his daughter meets him (11:34). Verse 39 says only that he 'did with her according to his vow', not explicitly that he burned her. Most readers ancient and modern (the Targum, the Midrash, most critical scholars) take it as a real sacrifice. Medieval commentators Kimhi and Gersonides read it as lifelong seclusion.
According to some commentators, among whom were Ḳimḥi and Levi b. Gershom, Jephthah only kept his daughter in seclusion.
it is taken for granted that Jephthah immolated his daughter on the altar
how the Bible does not command against child sacrifice.

✗ DOESN'T HOLD

The Bible does not command against child sacrifice and actually favours human sacrifice offered to its God.

The Bible prohibits it explicitly: 'thou shalt not let any of thy seed pass through the fire to Molech' (Leviticus 18:21), and Deuteronomy 12:31 calls burning sons and daughters an abomination. In Jeremiah 7:31 God says of the Tophet burnings, 'which I commanded them not, neither came it into my heart'. A real scholarly debate exists, built on texts such as Ezekiel 20:25-26 and the Jephthah and Isaac stories, about whether earlier Israelite religion tolerated it. The flat claim that no command against it exists is wrong.
not by works shall any should uh should any man that any man should boast

~ NARROWER

Paul taught that salvation is not by works, lest any man should boast.

The verse is Ephesians 2:8-9: 'Not of works, lest any man should boast'. Whether Paul wrote Ephesians is disputed; Raymond Brown estimated that about 80% of critical scholars think he did not. The undisputed letters make a similar case (Romans 3:20, 28), but Paul also writes that God 'will render to every man according to his deeds' (Romans 2:6).
about 80% of critical scholarship judges that Paul did not write Ephesians
as it is written, Jacob have I loved, Esau as I hated.

◇ INTERPRETATION

Romans 9 shows God planned before birth to hate Esau and his whole lineage with no chance of redemption.

The text is accurate: Romans 9:11-13 says, before the twins were born, 'Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated'. Paul is quoting Genesis 25:23 ('two nations are in thy womb') and Malachi 1:2-3, where Esau stands for the nation of Edom. Mainstream readings treat the passage as election of peoples to roles in history, with 'hated' as a Semitic idiom for 'not chosen'; Calvinist readings take it as individual predestination. 'No redemption for the whole lineage' goes beyond the text.
let's go to 2 Corinthians 12:7 where Paul admits to having a demon in his flesh

~ NARROWER

In 2 Corinthians 12:7 Paul admits to having a demon in his flesh, which shows his letters carry human, not only divine, input.

Paul says he was given 'a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me'. That is an affliction sent against him, not a statement that a demon lived in him. Proposed identifications include illness, persecution, opponents and a demonic attacker, and several commentators conclude it cannot be identified. The wider point, that Paul writes in a personal human voice, is plain from the passage.
Paul does not specify the nature of his 'thorn'.
sermons of Peter book two chapter 28 for the scriptures have joined to themselves many falsehoods

~ NARROWER

Peter, writing 2,000 years ago in a text present when the Bible was formed, said the scriptures had many falsehoods added to them.

The passage is real, but it is Homilies 2.38, not 2.28. It reads 'the Scriptures have had joined to them many falsehoods against God', and it also has the 'much safer to incur danger' line quoted at 1:42:59. It is the Peter of the pseudo-Clementine Homilies speaking, not Peter writing. The current consensus dates the Homilies to the fourth century, possibly drawing on a third-century source, so not 2,000 years ago.
the present consensus places these texts in the mid-fourth century, originating perhaps in Syria.
So right here he says the unnatural eating of flesh meats. He calls eating meat unnatural.

~ NARROWER

Peter in the Clementines calls flesh-eating 'unnatural' and as polluting as the heathen worship of devils.

This sentence is not in the held ANF translation of the Homilies; a search of the full text, including Homily XII, finds no 'unnatural' flesh-eating line. It circulates online attributed to 'Homily XII' via Keith Akers' A Vegetarian Sourcebook (1989), and reads like a modern summary. The Homilies do support a narrower version: converts are told 'to abstain from the table of devils, not to taste dead flesh, not to touch blood' (Homilies 7.4), and Peter says he eats 'only bread and olives' (12.6).
International Vegetarian Union, Clementine Homilies page
The unnatural eating of flesh meats is as polluting as the heathen worship of devils
there is not one scholar alive today who would say that Peter wrote second Peter.

✗ DOESN'T HOLD

No living scholar thinks Peter wrote 2 Peter, it dates to the early 3rd century, 3 John is no earlier than the 3rd century, and Acts is definitely 2nd century.

Most scholars do judge 2 Peter pseudepigraphal, but some still defend Peter's authorship, and estimates run from AD 60 to 150, not the 3rd century. 3 John is usually dated near the end of the 1st century (Dodd 96-110, Brown 100-110). Acts is usually dated 80-90; a growing minority prefers c. 110-120, which is a live debate rather than settled fact.
Scholars estimate the date of authorship anywhere from AD 60 to 150.
the epistle was likely written near the end of the first century.
The book is usually dated to 80–90 AD.
gospel of the Hebrews is very clear that uh that Jesus never claimed to be God

~ NARROWER

The Gospel of the Hebrews, suppressed and lost, clearly shows Jesus never claimed to be God, no Trinity, and a motherly Holy Spirit.

The motherly Spirit holds: Origen preserves Jesus saying 'my mother, the Holy Spirit, took me by one of my hairs'. But the gospel survives only in short quotations by church fathers, and no surviving fragment addresses whether Jesus claimed to be God or the Trinity, so 'very clear' overstates it. It fell out of use after the canon closed; no record says it was deliberately burned.
Even so did my mother, the Holy Spirit, take me by one of my hairs
All are known today only from fragments preserved in quotations by the early Church Fathers.

SAY IT CAREFULLY

The 'no blood offering of beast or bird or man' passage and the 'Israel of God' commandments read from the screen come from the Gospel of the Holy Twelve (Ouseley, 1898-1901), not an ancient gospel. The passage read at 50:32 is from the Essene Gospel of Peace (Szekely, 1937), a 20th-century composition. Neither should be cited as Jesus's words.

SAY IT CAREFULLY

Jeremiah 7:21 says 'eat flesh', not 'cease ye from the eating of flesh'. No manuscript supports the reading given at 06:13.

SAY IT CAREFULLY

The Clementine 'many falsehoods' passage is Homilies 2.38, not 'book two chapter 28'. It is not 2,000 years old; the consensus dates the Homilies to the 4th century.

SAY IT CAREFULLY

'The unnatural eating of flesh meats is as polluting as the heathen worship of devils' is not in the held Homilies text; do not quote it as Peter's words. Quote Homilies 7.4 ('not to taste dead flesh') instead.

SAY IT CAREFULLY

The judge in Judges 11 is Jephthah, not Jethro (Moses' father-in-law), though the captions may be to blame.

SAY IT CAREFULLY

3 John is not third-century and 2 Peter is not early third-century; both are usually dated between the late first and mid second centuries.

SAY IT CAREFULLY

'Over 32 billion animals in the United States alone' does not match the USDA count of land animals (about 9.2 billion slaughtered in 2015). A figure that large only appears if fish and shellfish are counted; one estimate gives 3.8 billion fish and 43.1 billion shellfish for 2013 (all-creatures.org, citing USDA and Counting Animals).

QUESTION TO EXPLORE

Jeremiah 7:22 says God did not command sacrifices at the Exodus, while Jeremiah 33:18 promises Levites to offer them forever. How did ancient Jewish and Jewish-Christian readers (for example Recognitions 1.36-37) reconcile the two?

QUESTION TO EXPLORE

If the Essenes broke with the Temple yet still legislated sacrifice (4QMMT, the Temple Scroll), what exactly did Philo mean by 'not sacrificing living animals'?

QUESTION TO EXPLORE

Homilies 2.38 and 3.42-51 offer a criterion for spotting 'false pericopes'. How does that criterion compare with this episode's 'God's character' test for which passages to keep?

QUESTION TO EXPLORE

Was Jephthah's daughter sacrificed or secluded, and why did medieval Jewish commentators read Judges 11:39 the way they did?

QUESTION TO EXPLORE

Does Jesus's 'least of these my brethren' (Matthew 25:40) have any ancient reading that extends it to animals, or is that a modern extension?
